clinicalPearls: A chronic, bilateral, often seasonally recurrent allergic keratoconjunctivitis affecting mainly children and young males, frequently with atopy
The palpebral form shows large cobblestone (giant) papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva
The limbal form shows gelatinous limbal papillae with white Horner-Trantas dots (collections of eosinophils and epithelial cells)
Intense itching, ropy mucoid discharge, photophobia, and tearing are characteristic symptoms

Corneal involvement ranges from punctate epithelial keratitis to a shield ulcer, a sterile oval epithelial defect in the superior cornea from inflammatory mediators and mechanical trauma from giant papillae
A shield ulcer can become plaque-covered and heal poorly, threatening the visual axis, and warrants more intensive treatment

Management uses allergen avoidance, topical mast cell stabilisers and antihistamines, topical corticosteroids for flares, and topical immunomodulators (calcineurin inhibitors) for steroid-sparing control
The condition tends to remit after adolescence but can leave limbal stem cell damage, scarring, or keratoconus in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic allergic inflammation of the ocular surface involving both IgE-mediated (type I) and cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity, with a prominent role for eosinophils, mast cells, and T lymphocytes. Repeated allergen exposure and chronic inflammation drive proliferation of the tarsal conjunctiva into giant cobblestone papillae and produce gelatinous limbal papillae with Horner-Trantas dots. Eosinophil-derived toxic mediators, together with mechanical rubbing by giant papillae, damage the corneal epithelium and can produce a sterile shield ulcer in the superior cornea. Chronic severe disease may injure the limbal stem cells and cause scarring, and eye rubbing contributes to associated keratoconus.
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting giant tarsal papillae, limbal papillae, and Horner-Trantas dots
Fluorescein staining to detect punctate keratopathy and shield ulcers
Conjunctival scraping or cytology showing eosinophils when the diagnosis is uncertain
Corneal topography to detect associated keratoconus
Assessment of limbal stem cell function in severe chronic disease
redFlags: Shield ulcer or plaque threatening the visual axis
Progressive corneal scarring or limbal stem cell failure
Development of keratoconus from chronic eye rubbing
Secondary microbial keratitis complicating an epithelial defect
reference.prognosis: The disease is usually self-limiting and tends to resolve after adolescence, but severe or poorly controlled cases can cause shield ulcers, corneal scarring, limbal stem cell damage, and keratoconus with lasting visual consequences.
pitfalls: Prolonged unmonitored topical steroid use causing glaucoma, cataract, or infection
Missing a shield ulcer and its threat to the visual axis
Overlooking associated keratoconus in a child who rubs the eyes
Attributing chronic itching solely to simple allergic conjunctivitis and underestimating corneal risk
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Advise allergen avoidance, cool compresses, ocular lubricants and cessation of eye rubbing as baseline measures
Use topical mast-cell stabilisers or dual-acting antihistamine and mast-cell stabilisers for ongoing control
Give short pulsed courses of topical corticosteroids for severe acute flares, monitoring intraocular pressure
Introduce topical calcineurin inhibitors such as ciclosporin or tacrolimus as steroid-sparing agents in severe or chronic disease
Treat a shield ulcer intensively with anti-inflammatory therapy, lubrication and antibiotic cover, with plaque debridement or surgery if it fails to heal
Monitor for steroid-induced glaucoma and cataract, and screen with corneal topography for associated keratoconus
Refer to ophthalmology and cornea services, reassuring that the disease usually remits after adolescence
